extracted.intended_audience: aspiring YA novelists and fiction writers (authors seeking to write or publish young adult novels)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluation criteria for crafting novels aimed at young adult readers (roughly ages 12–18), focused on voice, characterization, authenticity, age-appropriateness, subject matter, and market considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is YA fiction (target readership & themes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Young adult fiction targets readers aged 12–18 and follows teenage characters grappling with adolescence (relationships, identity, coming-of-age). Many YA works are 'problem novels' or 'coming-of-age' stories featuring intense emotions, existential angst, loss of innocence, and fundamental life change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a canonical test for whether a work fits YA: protagonist perspective (teen in the moment), themes of transition/identity, and emotional intensity. Examples cited: The Catcher in the Rye, Lord of the Flies, The Outsiders, The Fault in Our Stars, The Hate U Give, Divergent. Note: YA is a category (not a genre like romance or horror) and can appeal to readers of any age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t think of YA as ‘adult fiction that’s been dumbed-down’
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simplify language, plot, or style to 'talk down' to teen readers — YA should aspire to the same (or higher) literary standards as adult fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with full craft rather than truncating complexity for presumed teen comprehension. The post cites Francesca Lia Block as an example of sophisticated YA prose. Anti-pattern: intentionally simplified vocabulary or stripped-down ideas under the assumption teens can't handle nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure your characters are the right age
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should ideally be between 14 and 18 (high-school age) for YA; a 12-year-old is typically middle-grade, while a 19-year-old is often new adult or adult depending on content and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond raw age, consider narrator perspective: a story told by a teen experiencing events (or in the recent past) is YA; a story told by an adult reflecting on teen years is usually adult literature. Examples: Prep and The Virgin Suicides feature teen protagonists but are treated as adult literature because of adult narration. Use protagonist age and narrative stance as a criterion for YA classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on authenticity (teen POV & causal story development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write from a believable teen point of view 'in the moment' (not with adult hindsight) and ensure plot developments arise from intrinsic story causes rather than authorial convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity includes voice and story causality: relationships and plot twists must feel driven by characters and believable motivations. Cited editorial complaint: lack of causality where events (especially new relationships) happen because 'the author wants it to.' Anti-patterns: contrived plot turns, adult-filtered wisdom, emotionally false beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write fully-formed, three-dimensional characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must have depth, nuance, and internal complexity — avoid stereotyping or underdeveloped 'stock characters' (e.g., one-dimensional jock or bookish quiet kid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure wants, desires, feelings, and nuances are evident so characters don't feel like puppets. Give antagonists redeeming traits and protagonists flaws; avoid assuming high-school archetypes map directly onto a character without inner life. Quotations from editors emphasize that underdeveloped characters turn readers off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the right voice for your protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is the protagonist's personality manifested across every word on the page (not just dialogue). It is shaped by word choice, sentence and paragraph length, syntax, punctuation, and cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately craft voice to match character and perspective — don't default to stereotypical snark. Use techniques like repetition, casual diction, invented slang (with context), punctuation choices, and rhythm to convey personality. Examples explained: The Princess Diaries (repetition, casual words, caps for emphasis), Feed (apathetic/dispassionate diction, invented terms), The Hate U Give (cadence, slang, matter-of-fact tone). Analyze punctuation and sentence structure as part of voice. Anti-pattern: one-size-fits-all 'teen' voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write around heavy subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: YA can and often should include sex, drugs, strong language, and other 'heavy' topics because teens experience these things; avoid shying away from darker content solely because it feels adult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include heavy topics when they serve authenticity and the story's purpose; avoid gratuitous darkness intended only to shock. Acknowledge there is a threshold for 'too dark' — darkness must be purposeful and handled responsibly. Example: cautionary note referencing Zombie as an example of potentially 'too dark' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t write into trends (prioritize originality & passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trends in YA are fickle; writing to chase current market fads risks making a manuscript feel derivative by the time it reaches readers or agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write about subjects that genuinely excite you — passion and originality will make a stronger submission. Editors/agents dislike manuscripts that feel like thin imitations of bestselling trends (e.g., attempting to emulate Suzanne Collins or Veronica Roth). Anti-pattern: opening a manuscript that immediately reads like 'something similar' to a current hit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papa, don’t preach (avoid didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not set up characters or plots primarily to teach a moral lesson; didactic storytelling is detectable and off-putting to YA readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the character's journey and emotional truth rather than using plot as a vehicle for moral instruction. YA readers expect emotional honesty and relatable complexity — avoid contriving failures or lessons just to 'teach' the reader. Anti-pattern: characters who exist only to sell moral high ground or to resolve into tidy lessons.
